quizName: DMV Practice Test #13 20 Questions • Passing Score 16

questions.question: When should you increase your following distance?

options.text: When you can see the road through vehicles in front of you.
When the weather is pleasant and clear.

questions.explanation: Increase your following distance when conditions require longer stopping time. This includes heavy traffic, poor weather, nighttime driving, or when you cannot see past the vehicle ahead.

questions.question: When it is raining, what should you do?

options.text: Ride in the center of the lane.
Pull off the road until the rain stops.
Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the tire tracks left by cars.
questions.explanation: When rain starts, the road is very slippery. Oil from cars has not yet washed away. Riding in tire tracks left by cars is safest. The left tire track is often your best choice.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, which should you NOT do?

options.text: Avoid talking to the passenger while riding.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid talking to the passenger while riding.
questions.explanation: A passenger adds weight, so your motorcycle responds more slowly. You should ride slower, start slowing sooner, and increase your following distance. Always warn your passenger about road conditions ahead.

questions.question: When should a passenger mount a motorcycle?

options.text: As far back on the seat as possible.

questions.explanation: Passengers should mount only after the engine starts and the transmission is in neutral. They should sit as far forward as possible without blocking the rider's control. They should hold onto the rider's waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: What percentage of motorcycle-car crashes are caused by drivers failing to yield the right-of-way to riders?
questions.explanation: More than half of motorcycle-car crashes happen because drivers fail to properly yield the right-of-way to riders.

questions.question: A helmeted rider is _______ more likely to survive a crash than a rider without a helmet.
questions.explanation: Riders without helmets are three times more likely to die from head injuries in a crash than riders wearing helmets, regardless of speed.

questions.question: When turning left, what should you do?

options.text: Press both handgrips at the same time.

questions.explanation: To turn, your motorcycle must lean. Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn to make it lean that way.

questions.question: When crossing angled railroad tracks, how should you approach them?
questions.explanation: The safest way is to go straight in your lane. Turning to hit the tracks at a right angle is dangerous because it may push you into another lane.

questions.question: Without a helmet, a motorcycle rider is ________ more likely to suffer a critical head injury in a crash.
questions.explanation: Without a helmet, a rider is five times more likely to suffer a critical head injury in a crash.

questions.question: How should you swerve correctly?

options.text: Press the handle grip in the direction you plan to swerve.
Press the handle grip opposite to where you plan to swerve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handle grip in the direction you plan to swerve.
questions.explanation: To swerve, apply light pressure to the appropriate handle grip. To swerve left, press the left grip, then press the right to straighten out. To swerve right, press the right grip, then the left.

questions.question: How does a motorcycle's stopping distance compare to a car's stopping distance?

options.text: Cars need much longer to stop.
Cars need a little longer to stop.
Motorcycles and cars take about the same time to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Motorcycles and cars take about the same time to stop.
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, motorcycles and cars stop in about the same distance. However, wet or slippery pavement makes stopping much harder for motorcycles.

questions.question: How can you keep another vehicle from sharing your lane?

options.text: Ride in the middle of your lane.
Ride in the left portion of your lane.
Ride in the right portion of your lane.
Swerve from side to side in your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the middle of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane. This discourages car drivers from trying to share your lane.

questions.question: When riding on a slippery surface, what should you NOT do?
questions.explanation: On slippery surfaces, you should slow down, avoid sudden movements, and use both brakes gently. Do not brake suddenly.

questions.question: What is the best lane position for a motorcycle rider?

options.text: The left portion of the lane
The center portion of the lane
The right portion of the lane
There is no single best lane position for all situations.

questions.correctAnswerText: There is no single best lane position for all situations.
questions.explanation: The best lane position depends on your riding conditions. Choose a position that lets you keep a safe distance from other vehicles and stay visible to them.

questions.question: What should motorcycle riders do about hearing protection?

options.text: Wear hearing protection at all times to prevent hearing damage.
Wear hearing protection only on long rides.
Do not wear hearing protection because it will block horns and sirens.
Do not wear hearing protection if wearing a full-face helmet.

questions.correctAnswerText: Wear hearing protection at all times to prevent hearing damage.
questions.explanation: Wind and engine noise can damage your hearing permanently, even with a full-face helmet. Ear plugs protect your hearing while still letting you hear horns and sirens.

questions.question: What is one thing your riding clothes do NOT need to protect you from?
questions.explanation: Your riding clothes should protect you from sunburn, windburn, rain, dehydration, cold, and motorcycle parts. Good clothes also protect you in a crash.

questions.question: What should you do when a vehicle passes you from behind?

options.text: Move to the center of the lane.
Move to the left portion of the lane.
Move to the right portion of the lane.
Do not worry about which part of the lane you are in.

questions.correctAnswerText: Move to the center of the lane.
questions.explanation: When being passed, ride in the center of your lane. Staying too close to the passing vehicle increases the risk of a crash.

questions.question: Under ideal conditions, what is the minimum following distance you should maintain?
questions.explanation: Under normal conditions, keep at least two seconds of distance between you and the vehicle ahead. Increase this distance if conditions are worse.

questions.question: As your motorcycle's weight shifts forward during braking, what can you do?

options.text: Use less pressure on the front brake.

questions.explanation: As your weight moves forward during braking, the front wheel has more grip. This means you can press the front brake harder.

questions.question: What should you do to react faster to a hazard?

options.text: Always ride below the speed limit.
Keep your fingers ready on the clutch and brakes.
Shift into neutral when slowing down.

questions.correctAnswerText: Keep your fingers ready on the clutch and brakes.
questions.explanation: In high-risk areas like school zones or construction zones, keep your fingers ready on the clutch and brakes. This reduces your reaction time if a hazard appears.
